# Structure of Correlation Matrix

## Setting and definitions

Let $a = (a_1,\dots,a_n)$ and $b = (b_1,\dots,b_n)$ be sequences of $n$ real observations. For real sequences $x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)$, $y=(y_1,\dots,y_n)$ write
$$\bar x = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n x_i,\qquad \operatorname{cov}(x,y) = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y),\qquad \sigma_x = \sqrt{\operatorname{cov}(x,x)} .$$
(Note $\operatorname{cov}(x,x)=\frac1n\sum_i (x_i-\bar x)^2\ge 0$, so $\sigma_x$ is a well-defined non-negative real.) The (Pearson) correlation coefficient is
$$\rho(x,y) = \frac{\operatorname{cov}(x,y)}{\sigma_x\,\sigma_y},$$
which is defined exactly when $\sigma_x>0$ and $\sigma_y>0$, i.e. when neither sequence is constant. The correlation matrix of $a$ and $b$ is
$$\mathbf C = \begin{pmatrix} \rho(a,a) & \rho(a,b)\\ \rho(b,a) & \rho(b,b)\end{pmatrix},$$
i.e. with $x^{(1)}=a$, $x^{(2)}=b$, the entry in row $j$, column $k$ is $C_{jk}=\rho(x^{(j)},x^{(k)})$.

**Standing assumption.** For $\mathbf C$ to exist at all, every correlation coefficient in it must be defined, so $\sigma_a>0$ and $\sigma_b>0$ (neither sequence is constant). This is implicit in the hypothesis that $\mathbf C$ is the correlation matrix of $a$ and $b$.

**Remark on normalisation.** Some authors use $\frac1{n-1}$ instead of $\frac1n$ in the covariance (and hence in $\sigma$). If the factor is $c>0$ instead of $\frac1n$, then $\operatorname{cov}$ and $\sigma^2$ are both multiplied by the same constant $nc$, so $\sigma_x\sigma_y$ is multiplied by $\sqrt{nc}\sqrt{nc}=nc$ and $\rho$ is unchanged. Hence the argument below does not depend on this choice. The argument also works verbatim for the correlation matrix of any finite family $x^{(1)},\dots,x^{(m)}$ of non-constant sequences of length $n$.

## Proof

Let $x^{(1)},\dots,x^{(m)}$ be non-constant real sequences of length $n$ (for the statement, $m=2$, $x^{(1)}=a$, $x^{(2)}=b$), and $C_{jk}=\rho(x^{(j)},x^{(k)})$ for $1\le j,k\le m$. All these entries are defined because every $\sigma_{x^{(j)}}>0$.

**Step 1: covariance is symmetric.** For any sequences $x,y$ of length $n$,
$$\operatorname{cov}(x,y)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\bar y)(x_i-\bar x)=\operatorname{cov}(y,x),$$
by commutativity of multiplication of real numbers applied termwise.

**Step 2: $\mathbf C$ is symmetric.** For $1\le j,k\le m$, using Step 1 and commutativity of real multiplication in the denominator,
$$C_{jk}=\frac{\operatorname{cov}(x^{(j)},x^{(k)})}{\sigma_{x^{(j)}}\sigma_{x^{(k)}}}=\frac{\operatorname{cov}(x^{(k)},x^{(j)})}{\sigma_{x^{(k)}}\sigma_{x^{(j)}}}=C_{kj}.$$
Hence $\mathbf C^{\mathsf T}=\mathbf C$, i.e. $\mathbf C$ is symmetric. (For $m=2$: $\rho(a,b)=\rho(b,a)$.)

**Step 3: diagonal entries equal $1$.** For $1\le j\le m$, put $x=x^{(j)}$. By definition $\sigma_x=\sqrt{\operatorname{cov}(x,x)}$ with $\operatorname{cov}(x,x)\ge0$, so $\sigma_x^2=\operatorname{cov}(x,x)$. Since $x$ is non-constant, $\sigma_x>0$, so $\sigma_x^2\neq 0$ and
$$C_{jj}=\rho(x,x)=\frac{\operatorname{cov}(x,x)}{\sigma_x\sigma_x}=\frac{\sigma_x^2}{\sigma_x^2}=1.$$
(Why non-constant gives $\sigma_x>0$: $\sigma_x=0$ iff $\sum_i (x_i-\bar x)^2=0$ iff $x_i=\bar x$ for all $i$, since a sum of non-negative reals vanishes only if every term does; so $\sigma_x=0$ iff $x$ is constant.)

For $m=2$ this gives $\rho(a,a)=\rho(b,b)=1$.

Combining Steps 2 and 3,
$$\mathbf C=\begin{pmatrix}1 & \rho(a,b)\\ \rho(a,b) & 1\end{pmatrix},$$
which is symmetric with all main-diagonal entries equal to $1$. $\blacksquare$
